S2.F1.caption: (a) highly spiked
citing_paragraphs:
In this section, we analyze the weight statistics of three fine-tuned models when regularization is applied on: (a) only fully connected (FC) layers of Whisper-small, (b) all layers of Whisper-small, and (c) only FC layers of Whisper-medium. These models are referred to as Net-1, Net-2, and Net-3, respectively. In all models, the mean μ\mu and standard deviation σ\sigma of weights are in the order of 10−410^{-4} and 10−210^{-2}, respectively, in all layers (except LayerNorm in Net-2). We observe three main types of weight distributions, namely (A) highly spiked (Fig.1(a)), (B) narrowly spread (Fig.1(b)), and (C) widely spread (Fig.1(c)) distributions around mean. In highly spiked distributions (type A), the weights between the 25t​h25^{th} and 75t​h75^{th} percentiles, denoted by Q2,Q3Q_{2},Q_{3}, are in the order of 10−1110^{-11}. This implies that 50%50\% of the weights are very close to zero, and hence, can be pruned immediately. However, we prune all weights between μ−0.1​σ\mu-0.1\sigma and μ+0.1​σ\mu+0.1\sigma in order to prune more weights than those in the interquartile range. So, we set the threshold function as T1=0.1​σT_{1}=0.1\sigma. In narrowly spread distributions (type B), Q2,Q3Q_{2},Q_{3} are at ∼(μ±0.3​σ)\sim(\mu\pm 0.3\sigma). To prune slightly more weights than those in the inter-quartile range, the threshold function is set as T2=max⁡{|Q2|,|Q3|}T_{2}=\max\{|Q_{2}|,|Q_{3}|\}. The widely spread distributions (type C), have Q2,Q3Q_{2},Q_{3} locations at ∼(μ±0.67​σ)\sim(\mu\pm 0.67\sigma). We can not apply threshold to be max⁡{|Q2|,|Q3|}\max\{|Q_{2}|,|Q_{3}|\} as it will prune too many weights. Hence, we use the widely adopted threshold function, T3=η​Wm​a​xT_{3}=\eta W_{max} where Wm​a​xW_{max} is the maximum absolute weight of matrix WW and η>0\eta>0 is a hyperparameter [13].

We analyze the weight distributions of the columns of weight matrices in different layers. The columns that follow highly spiked distributions (type A), have weights very close to mean (∼0\sim 0) i.e., almost zero weights. To identify these weights, θ0\theta_{0} is set as 0.1​σc0.1\sigma_{c}. To prune columns with 90% approximate sparsity, θc\theta_{c} is set as 0.90.9 (see a sample pruned column weight distribution in Fig. 1(d)). The weights of the unpruned columns (a sample weight distribution shown in Fig. 1(e)) of a layer are further pruned in the second pass of pruning using a threshold θw\theta_{w}, which is set as T1,T2T_{1},T_{2} or T3T_{3}, depending on whether the layer follows distribution type A, B, or C. We observe the following weight distributions in Net-1, 2, and 3.
Net-1: The first 6 FC layers of the encoder have type A distributions, remaining encoder layers follow type B, while the decoder layers follow type C distributions.
Net-2: There are 3 FC + 7 attention (ATT) + 1 convolution (CONV) layers in the encoder, and 14 ATT + 2 FC layers in the decoder; i.e., a total of 27 layers (denoted by 𝒫1)\mathcal{P}_{1}), which exhibit distributions of type A. The remaining layers follow distributions of type C. The LayerNorm layers of both the encoder and decoder have significantly larger weights (μ∼1.0,σ∼10−1\mu\sim 1.0,\sigma\sim 10^{-1}) and hence, cannot be pruned.
Net-3: The first 5 layers of the encoder follow type A, while all the remaining layers of the encoder and decoder follow type B distribution. We apply the derived thresholds and provide results in the next section.

contextual_paragraphs.html: Loss regularization techniques such as weight decay or L1L_{1} norm minimization involves adding a penalty term on the magnitude of the weights to regularize the cross entropy function ℒC​E\mathcal{L}_{CE}. This falls in the category of regularized loss minimization, while just using ℒC​E\mathcal{L}_{CE} is empirical risk minimization. The sparsity induced by the L1L_{1} mechanism is unstructured, as the weights being driven to zero are randomly spread across the weight matrices. Pruning these parameters reduces memory requirement, but does not reduce FLOPs. In the context of statistical literature, Sparse Group LASSO (SGL) [14] was introduced where, an additional grouped loss regularization imposes structured sparsity on a group of weights as a whole. We exploit this SGL penalty function in our work to drive certain columns of weight matrices to zero. Let 𝐖j​l\mathbf{W}_{jl} be the jt​hj^{th} weight matrix of the lt​hl^{th} layer, with a total of JlJ_{l} matrices for 1≤l≤L1\leq l\leq L layers. Let 𝐖j​li\mathbf{W}_{jl}^{i} denote the it​hi^{th} column of 𝐖j​l\mathbf{W}_{jl} and IJlI_{J_{l}} denote the number of columns of each matrix 𝐖j​l\mathbf{W}_{jl}. Each such column 𝐖j​li\mathbf{W}_{jl}^{i} represents the set of outgoing connections from a neuron in layer jj to every neuron in the next layer j+1j+1. By imposing column-wise structured sparsity, the entire column can be pruned. These pruned columns are excluded from matrix multiplication, resulting in the reduction of FLOPs.
